Annual Crop Land: Annual Crop Land is a mosaic of rectangular or polygonal fields with sharp, straight boundaries and uniform sizes ranging from 0.5 to 5 hectares.
Annual Crop Land shows high geometric regularity in field layouts, with parallel and perpendicular edge alignments forming grid-like patterns.
Annual Crop Land displays dominant green hues varying in saturation depending on crop growth stage, but never uniformly brown or gray like fallow or built-up land.
Annual Crop Land exhibits fine-grained, homogeneous vegetation texture with consistent density across each field, lacking the clumpy or patchy distribution seen in pasture or orchard.
Annual Crop Land contains few or no permanent linear features such as paved roads crossing fields—access tracks are narrow, unpaved, and infrequent.
Annual Crop Land lacks visible buildings or built structures within field interiors, distinguishing it from mixed-use rural settlements.
Annual Crop Land has minimal or no surface water bodies—fields are dry or only show temporary irrigation channels, not persistent ponds or rivers.
Annual Crop Land features fields with smooth, flat surfaces showing no topographic relief or shadow variation indicative of hills or forests.
Annual Crop Land shows seasonal color shifts across adjacent fields—some green, some brown, some bare—reflecting staggered planting and harvest cycles.
Annual Crop Land contains no tree canopy cover; any vegetation appears low-statured and uniform in height, unlike orchards or agroforestry.
Annual Crop Land has field boundaries defined by thin, straight lines of bare soil or low vegetation, not hedgerows, trees, or stone walls.
Annual Crop Land exhibits high field-edge density per unit area, with many small-to-medium fields packed closely together without intervening natural land.
Annual Crop Land lacks the irregular, organic shapes and fragmented edges typical of forest clearings or abandoned land.
Annual Crop Land shows no evidence of permanent infrastructure such as power lines, large storage silos, or processing facilities embedded within fields.
Annual Crop Land has no visible rooftop geometry or impervious surface clusters that would indicate residential or industrial zones.
Annual Crop Land displays uniform spectral response within each field in multispectral bands, indicating single-species monoculture rather than mixed vegetation.
Annual Crop Land contains no linear drainage ditches with consistent width and curvature like those in rice paddies or wetland agriculture.
Annual Crop Land avoids the coarse, heterogeneous texture of scrubland or regenerating shrubland, maintaining fine-scale visual homogeneity within fields.
Annual Crop Land has no visible windbreaks, shelterbelts, or rows of mature trees separating fields, unlike some perennial crop systems.
Annual Crop Land shows no persistent snow cover or frozen ground patterns during winter months, as fields are typically tilled or left bare rather than insulated by vegetation.
Forest: Forest is dominated by irregularly shaped patches of dense green canopy with high texture variation and no visible geometric field patterns.
Forest has a continuous, unbroken canopy cover with minimal gaps larger than 10 meters across.
Forest exhibits high spatial heterogeneity in canopy height, visible as fine-grained brightness variation in near-infrared bands.
Forest contains sinuous, branching linear features consistent with natural river channels rather than straight, engineered canals.
Forest shows no aligned rows of crops or regularly spaced planting patterns typical of agricultural land.
Forest lacks the orthogonal street grids and rectilinear parcel boundaries characteristic of urban or suburban development.
Forest displays no visible paved roads wider than 5 meters or road networks with consistent spacing and right-angle intersections.
Forest has no discernible building footprints, even at high resolution, and zero structures exceeding 30 meters in length.
Forest contains no large, uniform water bodies such as rectangular reservoirs or canal-fed irrigation ponds.
Forest features organic, fractal-like canopy edges that contrast sharply with the smooth, curved boundaries of orchards or vineyards.
Forest shows no evidence of recent clear-cutting—no large contiguous bare-earth polygons adjacent to intact canopy.
Forest lacks the evenly spaced, repetitive dot pattern of mature tree plantations or commercial timber stands.
Forest contains abundant small-scale shadowing from multi-layered canopy, unlike the uniform shading of low shrubland or grassland.
Forest has no visible fence lines, property markers, or linear vegetation breaks indicating managed land division.
Forest exhibits high spectral contrast between adjacent pixels in red-edge bands due to dense, healthy chlorophyll-rich foliage.
Forest contains no regularly spaced, parallel linear gaps corresponding to logging skid trails or firebreaks.
Forest shows no mosaic of alternating green and brown patches indicative of rotational agriculture or fallow fields.
Forest has no clusters of circular or oval-shaped clearings associated with mining, drilling, or infrastructure sites.
Forest displays no alignment of canopy gaps following cardinal directions, distinguishing it from wind-thinned or plantation-edge effects.
Forest contains no high-reflectance linear features matching the spectral signature of concrete or asphalt roads cutting through vegetation.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land: Herbaceous Vegetation Land is dominated by a continuous, open expanse of low, uniform green texture without tree canopies or tall shrubs.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows irregular, organic patch boundaries rather than the straight-edged, geometric shapes typical of cultivated cropland.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land exhibits muted, medium-to-light green hues with minimal color variation, unlike the brighter, more saturated greens of intensively irrigated pasture.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land lacks visible linear infrastructure such as roads, field boundaries, or irrigation ditches that segment the surface.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land displays fine-grained, homogeneous vegetation texture without the coarse, clumpy or striped patterns seen in recently mowed or grazed grassland.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land contains no buildings, structures, or built surfaces, distinguishing it from rural residential or peri-urban land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has no standing water bodies, flooded areas, or discernible river channels crossing its extent.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows no evidence of regular planting rows, crop residue patterns, or soil tillage marks visible at satellite resolution.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land features soft, diffuse edges where it meets adjacent land classes, unlike the sharp, high-contrast boundaries of urban or agricultural land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land lacks the dense, repetitive dot-like patterns of scattered trees or shrubs characteristic of savanna or shrubland.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land appears uniformly matte in reflectance, without the specular highlights or directional sheen often present on wet or recently fertilized fields.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land occupies gently undulating or flat terrain with no visible terracing, contour plowing, or engineered slope modifications.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows no shadow-casting vertical elements such as isolated trees, utility poles, or wind turbines.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has no visible fencing, hedgerows, or other linear vegetation barriers dividing the area into parcels.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land displays consistent spectral response across its extent, lacking the patchy brightness variations caused by uneven grazing or drought stress in managed pasture.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land contains no discernible drainage networks, swales, or micro-topographic lineations indicating human hydrological intervention.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land lacks the angular, rectilinear fragmentation pattern associated with suburban or industrial development encroachment.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows no evidence of fire scars, recent burn lines, or ash-covered patches that would indicate recent disturbance.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land exhibits subtle tonal gradients corresponding to natural topography rather than the abrupt, uniform albedo shifts of paved or compacted surfaces.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has no visible access tracks, vehicle ruts, or narrow dirt paths cutting through the vegetation cover.
Highway or Road: Highway or Road is a long, straight or gently curved linear feature with consistent width and sharp, parallel edges.
Highway or Road is a dark gray or black ribbon-like feature flanked by lighter gray or tan shoulders or medians.
Highway or Road is a continuous linear feature that cuts directly across natural terrain features like hills, rivers, or forests without following their contours.
Highway or Road is a wide linear feature typically exceeding 20 meters in width, often with multiple parallel lanes visible as subtle tonal stripes.
Highway or Road is a geometrically precise linear feature aligned with cardinal directions or grid patterns more rigidly than local streets or trails.
Highway or Road is a linear feature with frequent, regularly spaced on-ramps and off-ramps forming perpendicular or acute-angle junctions.
Highway or Road is a linear feature bordered by sparse or absent vegetation, with abrupt transitions to adjacent land cover rather than gradual gradients.
Highway or Road is a linear feature that maintains uniform width and alignment over distances exceeding several kilometers without branching or narrowing.
Highway or Road is a linear feature exhibiting high spectral contrast against surrounding soil or pavement—darker than adjacent unpaved tracks or gravel roads.
Highway or Road is a linear feature with a central median strip—often light-colored or vegetated—that separates opposing traffic flows symmetrically.
Highway or Road is a linear feature that intersects other major roads at grade-separated interchanges with looping ramps, not simple crossroads.
Highway or Road is a linear feature surrounded by low building density immediately adjacent, unlike urban streets embedded within dense clusters of structures.
Highway or Road is a linear feature with minimal or no tree canopy coverage along its length, contrasting with shaded rural lanes or parkways.
Highway or Road is a linear feature that appears as a single dominant line in low-resolution imagery, whereas smaller roads fragment into discontinuous segments.
Highway or Road is a linear feature oriented orthogonally to regional topographic grain, unlike rivers which follow valleys or ridges.
Highway or Road is a linear feature with reflective surface properties causing bright linear highlights under direct sunlight, distinct from matte asphalt alleys or dirt paths.
Highway or Road is a linear feature bounded by engineered embankments or cut-and-fill slopes, visible as sharp elevation-related shadows or tonal shifts.
Highway or Road is a linear feature that consistently connects major population centers or infrastructure nodes, appearing as a primary corridor in regional-scale mosaics.
Highway or Road is a linear feature with service roads running parallel at regular intervals, creating a nested pair of linear elements separated by consistent spacing.
Highway or Road is a linear feature lacking intersecting field boundaries or property lines crossing it perpendicularly, unlike rural access roads dividing agricultural parcels.
Industrial Buildings: Industrial Buildings are large rectangular or L-shaped roof patches with sharp, straight edges and uniform gray or metallic tones.
Industrial Buildings occupy contiguous clusters of buildings covering more than 5 hectares with minimal intervening green space.
Industrial Buildings feature highly regular, grid-aligned building footprints arranged in parallel rows separated by wide, straight access roads.
Industrial Buildings show low vegetation density, typically less than 5% canopy cover across the entire parcel, with sparse, patchy grass or gravel surfaces.
Industrial Buildings have roofs dominated by smooth, reflective surfaces lacking texture variation, often appearing uniformly bright under sunlight.
Industrial Buildings contain numerous long, straight linear features including dual-lane service roads, rail spurs, and wide loading docks aligned orthogonally to building facades.
Industrial Buildings exhibit high building density with footprint coverage exceeding 70% of total parcel area, leaving little room for open ground.
Industrial Buildings display roof colors primarily in muted grays, silvers, or rust-brown tones, rarely incorporating red brick or warm earth tones.
Industrial Buildings lack visible tree canopies over structures and show no continuous tree-lined streets or perimeter groves.
Industrial Buildings contain large, unbroken paved areas such as parking lots or staging yards that exceed building footprint area by at least 1.5 times.
Industrial Buildings feature roof shapes dominated by flat or low-slope profiles with minimal gables, dormers, or pitched sections.
Industrial Buildings show no evidence of agricultural fields, crop rows, or irrigation patterns within their boundaries or immediate periphery.
Industrial Buildings are surrounded by wide, high-capacity arterial roads rather than narrow residential streets or winding rural lanes.
Industrial Buildings include large, unroofed storage yards with stacked shipping containers arranged in precise orthogonal grids.
Industrial Buildings lack rooftop solar panel arrays, residential chimneys, or visible HVAC units characteristic of commercial or residential buildings.
Industrial Buildings contain extensive networks of overhead utility lines and support towers running parallel to road edges, not seen in residential zones.
Industrial Buildings show no water bodies—neither ponds, retention basins, nor natural streams—within their operational boundaries.
Industrial Buildings have building heights consistently between one and three stories, with uniform roof elevations across adjacent structures.
Industrial Buildings feature large, unadorned wall surfaces with minimal fenestration, resulting in low visual texture complexity compared to mixed-use urban blocks.
Industrial Buildings are located on land with engineered, graded topography showing no natural slope variation or undulating terrain features.
Pasture Land: Pasture Land is a large, irregularly shaped patch of uniform greenish-yellow vegetation with low texture variation and no visible crop rows.
Pasture Land shows gently undulating terrain with soft, rounded field boundaries rather than sharp angular edges typical of cultivated cropland.
Pasture Land displays a homogeneous, fine-grained vegetation texture without the coarse, striped, or blocky patterns seen in tilled or harvested cropland.
Pasture Land has muted, medium-saturation green tones lacking the vivid spring green of young cereal crops or the brownish tinge of fallow fields.
Pasture Land contains sparse or absent linear field boundaries compared to the dense, rectilinear grid of hedgerows or irrigation ditches in intensively managed farmland.
Pasture Land exhibits minimal internal geometric structure, contrasting with the highly regular, rectangular parcel layouts common in orchard or vineyard land.
Pasture Land lacks the high-density clusters of farm buildings and storage structures found in mixed arable-livestock farms.
Pasture Land features few or no visible access roads crossing its interior, unlike pasture-integrated dairy farms which show branching gravel tracks.
Pasture Land shows no evidence of parallel furrows, ridges, or tillage marks that distinguish plowed cropland.
Pasture Land contains no regularly spaced tree canopies or aligned rows characteristic of silvopasture or agroforestry systems.
Pasture Land appears as contiguous grassland with no interspersed bare soil patches larger than 5 meters across, unlike recently grazed or overgrazed rangeland.
Pasture Land has smooth, continuous tonal gradients without abrupt color transitions indicating recent mowing or baling operations.
Pasture Land lacks the reflective linear strips of plastic mulch or drip irrigation tape visible in high-value horticultural land.
Pasture Land shows no standing water bodies or engineered drainage channels that distinguish wetland pasture from dry upland pasture.
Pasture Land contains no visible livestock clustering or movement trails concentrated near water points, unlike rangeland with scattered watering infrastructure.
Pasture Land displays consistent vegetation height and density across slopes, unlike erosion-prone hillside cropland with visible gullies or terracing.
Pasture Land has no perimeter fencing lines detectable as thin, straight dark lines—unlike newly established or subdivided pasture parcels.
Pasture Land shows no seasonal harvesting artifacts such as windrows, swaths, or hay bales scattered across the surface.
Pasture Land lacks the geometric repetition of solar panels, greenhouses, or poultry sheds found in diversified agricultural complexes.
Pasture Land presents a single dominant vegetation layer without vertical structural heterogeneity like scattered shrubs or isolated trees seen in woodland pasture.
Permanent Crop Land: Permanent Crop Land is characterized by regularly spaced, evenly sized circular or oval tree canopies forming a grid-like pattern across the field.
Permanent Crop Land shows high-density, uniform vegetation texture with consistent green tonal values year-round due to perennial woody plants.
Permanent Crop Land displays narrow, straight, parallel access rows between crop rows, visible as fine linear gaps in the canopy cover.
Permanent Crop Land exhibits rectangular or square field boundaries aligned to cardinal directions with sharp, unbroken edges.
Permanent Crop Land contains no visible seasonal bare soil patches, unlike annual cropland which shows large brown or tilled areas during off-seasons.
Permanent Crop Land has uniformly low canopy height variation, producing smooth, even spectral texture in near-infrared reflectance.
Permanent Crop Land lacks the irregular, fragmented patchwork of mixed vegetation and built structures seen in rural residential land.
Permanent Crop Land shows minimal or no visible irrigation ditches compared to rice paddies, which display dense networks of water-filled linear features.
Permanent Crop Land features sparse road density—typically only one or two unpaved service roads per large field unit.
Permanent Crop Land contains no visible row-crop planting patterns such as alternating light-dark stripes caused by directional tillage or young annual crops.
Permanent Crop Land displays higher canopy closure than pastureland, with little to no exposed ground visible between individual plants.
Permanent Crop Land has consistent inter-canopy spacing that remains stable across seasons, unlike orchards undergoing replanting which show scattered bare patches.
Permanent Crop Land lacks the geometrically complex, small-scale parcel divisions typical of smallholder mixed farming systems.
Permanent Crop Land shows no evidence of recent mechanical disturbance like plowed furrows, harrow marks, or tractor tracks common in cultivated annual fields.
Permanent Crop Land contains no standing water bodies or flooded compartments, distinguishing it from aquaculture or rice-growing areas.
Permanent Crop Land exhibits uniform canopy shadow patterns under oblique sun angles, indicating consistent plant height and spacing.
Permanent Crop Land has no visible grain storage structures, silos, or large farm machinery sheds commonly found in intensive cereal production zones.
Permanent Crop Land displays minimal building footprint density—typically zero or only one small operational structure per several hectares.
Permanent Crop Land shows no linear hedgerows or irregular tree lines separating fields, unlike woodland-fragmented agricultural mosaics.
Permanent Crop Land maintains continuous, high-contrast green spectral signature in summer NDVI, exceeding the lower and more variable values of shrubland or degraded rangeland.
Residential Buildings: Residential Buildings are characterized by clusters of small to medium-sized rectangular or L-shaped building footprints arranged in irregular but loosely grid-like patterns separated by narrow streets.
Residential Buildings feature low-to-medium building density with significant interspersed open space occupied by individual lawns, gardens, and scattered trees.
Residential Buildings exhibit a patchy spatial distribution where built-up areas alternate with vegetated parcels, creating a mottled texture at medium resolution.
Residential Buildings show curvilinear street networks with cul-de-sacs and branching lanes, contrasting with the rigid orthogonal grids typical of commercial districts.
Residential Buildings contain numerous small, discrete impervious surfaces—each corresponding to a single-family dwelling—rather than large contiguous rooftops seen in industrial zones.
Residential Buildings display high edge density due to the abundance of building perimeters relative to total area, exceeding that of agricultural fields but less than dense urban cores.
Residential Buildings have rooftops predominantly in muted reds, grays, and tans, distinct from the uniform silvers and blues of warehouse complexes.
Residential Buildings include narrow, unpaved or lightly paved service roads that branch off main arterials, unlike the wide, multi-lane highways bounding transportation corridors.

Residential Buildings show moderate vegetation cover with fine-grained, heterogeneous tree canopies distributed individually or in small groups rather than continuous forest canopy or uniform crop rows.
Residential Buildings occupy patches typically ranging from 0.5 to 5 hectares in size, smaller than institutional campuses but larger than isolated farmsteads.
Residential Buildings lack large, uninterrupted paved surfaces such as airport runways or logistics yard expanses, instead featuring fragmented pavement networks.
Residential Buildings contain frequent small water features including backyard swimming pools, ornamental ponds, and stormwater retention basins absent in most rural residential subdivisions.
Residential Buildings exhibit low-rise verticality with roof heights rarely exceeding two stories, visually distinguishable from the taller, slab-like profiles of apartment towers.
Residential Buildings show irregular lot boundaries with variable setbacks, contrasting with the uniform parcel dimensions of planned industrial parks.
Residential Buildings have minimal linear infrastructure beyond local streets—no rail lines, transmission corridors, or major pipelines crossing the patch interior.
Residential Buildings display low spectral contrast between rooftops and adjacent paved surfaces, unlike the sharp reflectance differences between metal roofs and gravel lots in industrial yards.
Residential Buildings contain abundant small-scale linear shadows cast by individual trees and low buildings, producing a dappled shadow pattern unlike the long, uniform shadows of high-rises.
Residential Buildings feature detached or semi-detached structures with visible gaps between footprints, distinguishing them from the abutting facades of downtown row housing.
Residential Buildings show sparse vehicular infrastructure—few parking lots larger than 10 cars—and no loading docks or freight-handling zones.
Residential Buildings lack large, geometrically precise open spaces like sports fields or golf courses, instead containing irregularly shaped private yards and play areas.
River: River is a narrow, sinuous, dark blue or black linear feature with smooth, continuous edges and variable width that follows a winding path across the landscape.
River is a long, curving strip of water that contrasts sharply with adjacent land in both color and texture, appearing darker and smoother than surrounding soil or vegetation.
River is a linear water body that maintains consistent width over short distances but gradually widens or narrows along its course, unlike the abrupt terminations of lakes or ponds.
River is a dark, reflective line that often branches into smaller tributaries, forming a dendritic pattern distinct from the isolated, closed shapes of lakes.
River is a fluid, meandering corridor of water that cuts through diverse land covers—such as forest, cropland, or urban areas—without conforming to human-made grid patterns.
River is a linear feature with high spectral contrast against dry land, exhibiting strong near-infrared absorption and visible-band darkness not seen in roads or railways.
River is a continuous, unbroken waterway that flows downhill, visibly connecting upstream and downstream segments without interruption by dams or reservoirs in its natural state.
River is a dark, elongated feature whose banks often show subtle vegetated margins—narrow strips of green—distinguishing it from wider, uniformly dark water bodies like reservoirs.
River is a linear element that frequently crosses under or over roads and railways, creating clear overpass/underpass intersections visible as breaks in those features but not in the river itself.
River is a water feature with irregular, organic curvature and asymmetrical bends, unlike the straight or gently arced geometry of canals or irrigation ditches.
River is a dynamic water body whose surface reflects sky conditions, appearing bright on cloudy days and deep black on clear days—unlike the static, uniform brightness of paved roads.
River is a linear feature that commonly occupies low-lying topographic depressions, visible as subtle trough-like alignments in terrain texture or shadow patterns.
River is a dark, flowing watercourse that lacks parallel embankments or engineered margins, distinguishing it from artificial channels bounded by straight, light-colored berms.
River is a water feature that exhibits branching complexity at multiple scales, with primary, secondary, and tertiary channels forming hierarchical networks absent in isolated wetlands.
River is a linear water body whose width increases gradually downstream, producing a tapering visual signature unlike the uniform width of man-made drainage ditches.
River is a dark, continuous line that often snakes between hills or through valleys, following natural contours rather than cutting across them like major highways.
River is a water feature whose surface shows subtle flow-induced texture—slight ripples or streaks—in high-resolution imagery, unlike the still, glassy appearance of ponds.
River is a linear element that intersects agricultural fields at oblique angles, disrupting field boundaries rather than aligning with them like field drainage channels.

River is a dark, fluid corridor that frequently hosts islands or sandbars—small, light-toned patches within its dark expanse—unlike the homogeneous darkness of narrow streams without sediment deposition.
River is a water body whose banks display transitional zones of moisture-tolerant vegetation—thin, irregular green fringes—distinct from the abrupt, sharp edges of concrete-lined canals.
Sea or Lake: Sea or Lake is a large, contiguous expanse of dark blue to deep teal water with no visible vegetation or built structures within its boundaries.
Sea or Lake is a water surface that occupies the majority of the image frame and exhibits smooth, featureless texture without internal linear patterns.
Sea or Lake is a body of water with irregular, highly convoluted shorelines that lack straight edges or right-angle corners.
Sea or Lake is a water surface that reflects sky tones and shows variable brightness due to sun glint, unlike the uniform matte appearance of bare soil.
Sea or Lake is a water surface that lacks any visible river inflows or outflows connecting it to other water bodies in the same scene.
Sea or Lake is a water surface that appears darker than adjacent wetlands due to greater depth and lower sediment load.
Sea or Lake is a water surface that shows no evidence of grid-like field boundaries, unlike agricultural land.
Sea or Lake is a water surface that has no discernible road networks, building footprints, or paved surfaces intersecting or embedded within it.
Sea or Lake is a water surface whose edges transition abruptly to non-water land cover without gradual vegetation gradients typical of marshes.
Sea or Lake is a water surface that lacks the fine-scale mottled texture of shallow tidal flats or exposed mudflats.
Sea or Lake is a water surface that displays no persistent foam lines, breaking waves, or surf zones along its shoreline, distinguishing it from ocean coastlines with active wave action.
Sea or Lake is a water surface that appears uniformly continuous across its extent, without the fragmented, disconnected patches characteristic of small ponds or reservoirs.
Sea or Lake is a water surface that shows no evidence of aquaculture pens, floating platforms, or moored vessels at discernible scale.
Sea or Lake is a water surface that lacks the geometric regularity of irrigation canals or drainage ditches crossing through it.
Sea or Lake is a water surface that does not contain islands larger than a few pixels in area, unlike archipelagic or highly fragmented inland seas.
Sea or Lake is a water surface that exhibits no visible sediment plumes or turbid runoff entering from adjacent land, indicating stable, non-erosional boundaries.
Sea or Lake is a water surface that has no visible dam structures, spillways, or engineered embankments defining its perimeter.
Sea or Lake is a water surface that lacks the seasonal variation in extent visible as recurring dry margins or exposed lakebeds in arid regions.
Sea or Lake is a water surface that shows no evidence of submerged vegetation canopies or floating macrophyte mats that would break up its surface continuity.
Sea or Lake is a water surface that appears optically deep enough to suppress visibility of the bottom, unlike shallow coastal lagoons or flooded fields where substrate texture is partially visible.
